newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees say hundreds of thousands still in forest.
newsitem.headline: Refugees say hundreds of thousands still in forest.

text.p: Rwandan refugees who fled Katale camp last month began emerging from the forests of eastern Zaire on Saturday, telling of hundreds of thousands of their compatriots left behind.
"Imagine the population of Katale and Kahindo, all put in the same place, all together," said Jeanepo Musivimu, a Rwandan Hutu refugee from Kigali. "That is what it is like in the forest."
The combined populations of Katale and Kahindo camps was 310,000, according to UNHCR.
His testimony adds credence to the estimates of aid organisations, who say there are still possibly hundreds of thousands of refugees trying to make their way home after two years in exile.
Their flight was sparked by a Tutsi-led rebellion in eastern Zaire which routed Zairean government troops and the Interahamwe militia which had an iron grip on the vast refugee camps in the region.

Musivimu was talking on the outskirts of Mugunga camp, near Goma, after walking for seven days with his family. He had settled down with a group of other refugees for the night, intending to board a UNHCR bus for Goma at first light.

"There are so many people in the forest that it is impossible to describe," he said. "Along the way are many people who are sick and some who have been attacked. Many of the people are unaccompanied children whose parents have been killed."
During his flight he had lived on a handful of maize, roots and rain water.
Other refugees among the estimated 3,000 who arrived in Mugunga on Saturday told similar stories.
Francois Hakizimana drank nothing but rain water for two weeks and on Saturday lay almost completely dehydrated on a sheet of cardboard at a Red Cross way-station in Mugunga.
"There are hundreds like him now," said Bushiri Makangile, a local Red Cross volunteer, as he inserted a second drip into Hakizimana's arm.
"Our big worry is that there must be thousands of dead and dying out there and we can't get to them."
Hakizimana lay wearing all his clothes -- two anoraks, a sweater, three t-shirts and a shirt. Incapable of moving, he lay still as flies crawled in and out of his nostrils and mouth.
Next to him his brother fanned him with a cloth, while wearing an orange woollen overcoat, full of holes. "I bought it in Ruhengeri in winter 1993. We hope to be back there soon."
Around Hakizimana was the deserted remains of Mugunga camp, pillaged and wrecked. The air was full of the smell of decaying human excrement, eucalyptus woodsmoke and old sweat.
Empty purple bottles of Dear Heart Luxury Body lotion lay next to a broken trombone case, lined with torn indigo velveteen soaked by recent rain.
Refugees continued to arrive in Mugunga until dark fell, when the entire road to Goma lay empty.
